subject: physiology
title: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potentials, and Cutaneous Mechanoreceptors

steps.tx: Sensory receptors act as biological transducers that convert diverse mechanical, thermal, chemical, or electromagnetic physical stimuli into local electrochemical responses. When an adequate stimulus deforms or alters the receptor membrane, opening of non-selective cation channels generates a graded, non-propagated depolarisation termed the **receptor potential**, whose amplitude varies in direct proportion to stimulus intensity.
steps.say: A receptor potential is a graded depolarisation produced when an adequate stimulus opens cation channels.

nodes.label: Physical Modality Stimulates Specialized Receptor Ending or Sense Organ
Direct Stretch or Chemical Gating Opens Non-Selective Inward Cation Pores
Graded Local Receptor Potential Spreads Electrotonically Along Terminal
Reaches Trigger Zone Threshold to Fire Frequency-Coded Action Potentials

steps.tx: When maintained under continuous constant-strength stimulation, sensory receptors exhibit a progressive decline in receptor potential amplitude and afferent action potential firing frequency over time. This physiological damping is designated **sensory receptor adaptation**, allowing the nervous system to filter out continuous unvarying baseline background signals while remaining exquisitely sensitive to dynamic environmental changes.
steps.say: Receptor adaptation diminishes discharge frequency over time under constant stimulation, filtering unchanging signals.

left.title: Phasic (Rapidly Adapting) Receptors
points: Fire brief bursts of action potentials at stimulus onset and offset
Discharge frequency ceases completely during sustained steady stimulus
Specialized for detecting velocity, acceleration, and vibration
Examples include Pacinian corpuscles and Meissner corpuscles

right.title: Tonic (Slowly Adapting) Receptors
points: Fire continuously throughout prolonged duration of maintained stimulus
Discharge rate declines only modestly over seconds or minutes
Specialized for signaling static position, pressure, and stretch
Examples include Merkel discs, Ruffini endings, and muscle spindles

steps.tx: Under a steady stimulus, receptor potential amplitude and afferent firing both decline over time. That damping is **sensory receptor adaptation**. It lets the nervous system ignore an unchanging background and stay sensitive to what changes. The law of specific nerve energies is a separate rule about identity, not about fading. However a given sensory pathway is stimulated, mechanically, electrically, or by its natural stimulus, the sensation that results is the modality that pathway is built to report.
steps.say: Constant stimulation makes the receptor potential and the afferent firing rate fall, which is adaptation, so steady background is filtered out. Specific nerve energies answer another question. A pathway reports its own modality no matter whether the stimulus is its natural one, a mechanical poke, or an electric shock.

vis.alt: One sensory pathway giving the same modality whether it is stimulated naturally, mechanically, or electrically.
vis.caption: Whatever stimulus hits a given sensory nerve, the sensation reported is the modality that pathway is built to carry. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Regardless of how a specific sensory afferent pathway is stimulated, the perceived conscious sensation corresponds invariably to the normal modality mediated by that pathway. Formulated as the **law of specific nerve energies**, this principle dictates that electrical or mechanical irritation of the optic nerve produces visual flashes of light rather than sounds or tactile sensations.
steps.say: Muller law of specific nerve energies dictates that stimulating a sensory pathway always produces its specific modality.

vis.caption: Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring tracing specific modality-dedicated dorsal column and spinothalamic signals.
vis.alt: Sensory evoked potential electrophysiological tracings demonstrating pathway specificity

steps.tx: Perceptual psychophysics demonstrates that the perceived sensory intensity does not scale linearly with stimulus magnitude, but rather corresponds to a logarithmic mathematical function. Stated as the **Weber-Fechner law**, the just-noticeable difference between two sensory stimuli represents a constant ratio of the original baseline stimulus intensity across varying sensory modalities.
steps.say: The Weber-Fechner law states that perceptual sensory intensity scales logarithmically with physical stimulus magnitude.

steps.tx: Located deep within the subcutaneous tissue, joints, and mesentery, large concentric lamellar structures encasing a central unmyelinated axon terminal form the **Pacinian corpuscle**. Mechanical indentation of the fluid-filled onion-skin capsule redistributes viscoelastically within milliseconds, making this receptor extraordinarily rapidly adapting and tuned specifically to detect high-frequency vibration between one hundred and four hundred hertz.
steps.say: Pacinian corpuscles have fluid-filled lamellae that adapt rapidly to detect high-frequency vibration.

nodes.label: High-Frequency Mechanical Vibration (100-400 Hz) Indents Outer Capsule
Concentric Lamellae Slip, Transmitting Rapid Transient Pressure Wave
Terminal Axon Membrane Deforms, Opening Mechanosensitive Cation Channels
Intracapsular Fluid Instantly Redistributes, Dissipating Static Pressure

steps.tx: In glabrous non-hairy skin such as fingertips, lips, and palms, elongated encapsulated corpuscles nestled within the superficial dermal papillae serve as tactile sensors. These structures are **Meissner corpuscles**, which possess small receptive fields with distinct sharp boundaries and rapid adaptation, making them exquisitely suited for signaling dynamic skin movement, slip, and low-frequency flutter.
steps.say: Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae of glabrous skin adapt rapidly to detect light flutter and slip.

left.title: Meissner Corpuscle Properties
points: Located in superficial dermal papillae immediately beneath epidermis
Small receptive field (3 to 5 mm) with sharp defined borders
Rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor (RA1 sensory afferent unit)
Detects dynamic skin slip, grip friction, and flutter (20-50 Hz)

right.title: Merkel Disc Properties
points: Located at basal layer of epidermis aligned with dermal ridges
Small receptive field (2 to 4 mm) with highly localized boundaries
Slowly adapting type 1 mechanoreceptor (SA1 sensory afferent unit)
Detects sustained light pressure, fine textures, edges, and form

steps.tx: Positioned directly at the base of the epidermis in both hairy and glabrous skin, specialized neuroendocrine-like epithelial cells form synaptic contacts with expanded nerve terminals termed the **Merkel disc**. Because they adapt slowly and express mechanosensitive Piezo two channels, Merkel complexes discharge continuously to sustain fine tactile discrimination of fine textures, curves, and sharp edges.
steps.say: Merkel discs at the epidermal base adapt slowly to signal sustained pressure, edges, and fine surface textures.

vis.caption: Cutaneous sensory nerve fiber degeneration causing loss of distal vibratory and fine tactile sensation.
vis.alt: Peripheral sensory axon loss and distal sensory receptor impairment

steps.tx: The density of primary mechanoreceptor innervation across the cutaneous surface determines the peripheral spatial resolution of the nervous system. Body areas dedicated to fine manipulation such as the fingertips and tongue exhibit dense receptor packing with minimal convergence, whereas proximal trunk skin displays sparse innervation and broad receptive fields that diminish tactile **two-point spatial discrimination**.
steps.say: High receptor density and small receptive fields in fingertips enable sharp two-point spatial discrimination.

nodes.label: Fingertip and Lip Skin Displays Extremely Dense Mechanoreceptor Arrays
Primary Afferents Form Tiny Receptive Fields with Minimal Central Convergence
Calipers Separated by Only 2 Millimeters Readily Perceived as Two Distinct Points
